segments.text: Let's now take a look at addressing the
N + 1 problem in SQL Alchemy when it
comes to related objects. So what we
have here is a statement. We're
selecting a movie from the database and
let's say we want to get one of these
movies. So if we look at the data we
have here, let's say we want to get Blue
Velvet. So I'm going to copy the name of
that. Now we could get this in various
ways. For example, if we know the ID is
10, what we could do is go back here and
we could use that method we found out
about before, which was session.get and
we could pass in the movie and the ID of
10 there. But let's assume we don't know
that. We only have the name and we want
to use the .where function and we then
say that we want the movie where
movie.name is equal to Blue Velvet. And
remember we have a filter by convenience
function that we can also use here, but
I'm going to stick to this where
function here. So we have a selection
there and then we can manifest that
result into a movie instance by calling
session.scalar
and that will give us back to the object
and we can print that object below and
you see the movie Blue Velvet. Now I'm
going to add another print statement
here and we're going to access
movie.reviews which remember is the
relationship field and that will give us
all of the reviews associated with Blue
Velvet. Now the interesting thing about
this is if we go back to the top and we
turn echo on on the SQL Alchemy engine.
So let's turn echo on and go back to the
bottom here. Now what happens when we
execute this code? The first statement
here will get the movie with the name
that is passed in by the engine. In this
case that's Blue Velvet as you can see
here. And then after that on this line
of code here when we actually access
movie.reviews which remember is a
relationship field, SQL Alchemy's
session then issues another select query
to get all reviews that have a movie ID
equal to the ID that is passed in by the
engine for Blue Velvet. In this case
that is 10. So there's a second
selection to get all of the reviews and
that's because the related objects are
lazily loaded. And that's not a big
problem here for a single movie, but
imagine we are pulling out multiple
movies from the database. So get rid of
this where clause here. And instead of
session.scalar, we're going to change
that to the scalars method. So, instead
of the first row and the first column,
that's going to return the first column
for all of the rows that are returned by
this. So, we're going to get back a
number of movie instances. So, let's
rename the variable as movies here. And
what we're going to do below is we're
going to iterate over each of these
movies. And let's move this print
statement in here. So, we're going to
print the reviews inside the for loop.
So, let's execute this and we can see
what comes back here. Now, notice how
much SQL is being sent here. And in
fact, this is being truncated. So,
what's happening if we look here is that
we get back all of the reviews with this
line of code and this selection. And if
we look in the database, you can see we
have eight movies here. So, it gets back
all of those. And then we iterate over
each one of those one at a time. So, if
we look in the database, you can see we
have eight movies here. It gets all of
those. And then we have a for loop. And
this is iterating eight times, one for
each movie. And every time it lazily
accesses that reviews property, it's
going to issue another selection to get
all of the reviews associated with the
movie that we are iterating over. And
because we have eight movies, we then
end up sending eight separate SQL
statements to the database to get the
associated reviews. Now, this is the n +
1 problem and it's a common performance
issue in applications. So, the n + 1
comes from the fact that we issue one
select query to get all movies. And then
for every single movie that we have, we
then issue another query for each one of
those to get the associated reviews. n
queries for each movie plus the one
query to get all of the initial movies
from the database. Now, we can mitigate
this using a join, but there are better
strategies when working with the ORM.
But this problem of lazy loading and
then accessing in a loop, it's one of
the most famous ORM patterns. And I say
famous and I mean that in a negative way
because it can really affect performance
in applications. But this code looks
innocuous enough that you don't really
know unless you know what you're doing
that this is problematic. And if you
want to know why it's problematic,
usually in a database table, you might
have thousands, potentially tens of
thousands or more rows, and iterating
over those and issuing further select
queries which then have to be sent to
the database, which then processes the
query and sends back the results. That
is not the most effective way of doing
this. You want to cut down on the number
of round trips to a database, and the n
plus one query will kill performance for
any kind of data where you don't have a
trivial number of rows in the initial
select. So let's look now at a common
strategy to reduce these unnecessary
selects. If we go back to model.py, when
we have a movie object, we get the
reviews here, and we can actually add a
parameter to the relationship. So we're
going to come back to that later on, but
for now, let's go back to the notebook,
and we're going to add a loader strategy
to the select query that we have here.
And we can do this using a method called
.options, and we'll explain what's going
on in a second. At the top, from
sqlalchemy.orm,
we're going to import one of these
loader options, and it's called select
and load. So let's take the name of
that, and we're going to pass that into
the options method, and we can pass in
as a parameter to select and load the
reviews relationship. Now if we go back
down here, we are hopefully going to see
that this greatly cuts down on the
number of SQL queries that are issued to
the database just by adding that option,
that loader strategy called select and
load. So let's execute this, and if we
go down here, you can see we have much
less code. So there's a lot less SQL
being sent to the database. We still get
some output here, but that's actually
coming from a print statement within the
iteration that we're doing over the
movies. But we're now using this loader
strategy called select and load. And
let's have a look at what's actually
going on in the SQL queries. And notice
here we get all of the movies. That's
the query that we were issuing before
that gives us back all eight movies from
the database. And then here we have a
different query than before. We're
getting all reviews where the review
movie ID is in this set of parameters,
and those parameters are from the
initial query over the movies. So
basically, the ORM is extracting all of
the IDs from the initial query, and
instead of one per ID, we can then use
the IN statement in SQL and pass them
all in and get back all reviews that are
attached to one of those IDs in a single
SQL query. That's the behavior of select
and load. And we can go to the
documentation on loader strategies,
which I'll leave a link to below the
video. Now, if we go down here, you can
see that loader strategies are
represented as objects that may be
associated with select statements using
select.options method, which we have
just used. And if we scroll down
further, we're going to see what the
select and load strategy is going to do.
Now, as it says here, this is the most
useful loader in modern SQL Alchemy, and
it solves the most common form of the N
+ 1 problem. So what select and load
does is it ensures that a particular
collection for a full series of objects
are loaded up front using a single
query. And that's what's going on here
in this SQL that we see here. We're
getting all reviews and we're doing that
in a single query based on the movie IDs
that were collected in the initial
select statement. And that happens
transparently when we use select and
load. So behind the scenes, it's doing
all of that collection of all of the
movie IDs that have been fetched and
then attaching them to this subsequent
query to get back the reviews. And
there's no join statement here that's
been introduced. We have instead two
select queries. The first one gets all
of the movies, and the second one will
then fetch all reviews that are
associated with the set of movie IDs
that were originally fetched. So before
with eight movies, we had nine total
queries with the N + 1 problem. We've
cut that down from nine to two queries.
Now we can see all of the movie IDs that
are passed in here. We could explicitly
get a subset of movies here using the
dot where function that we've seen
before. And I'm going to pass in
movie.id. Now remember from the column
that we've seen before, we have an IN
method and we can pass to that a list of
IDs in this case. So for example, if we
want to get only the movies whose ID is
one of these values, we can use this in
the where clause. So we reference the
movie dot ID column and we use the in
function to pass in the set of values we
want to fetch. So if we execute this
code here, notice that the statement
below, and it's this one here where we
fetch the associated reviews, it only
now does so for the movies that have
those IDs. So those IDs are passed in
automatically when we used the select
and load strategy when it's fetching the
associated reviews for those movies. And
this is where the select and load name
comes from. And it's the fact that it
uses the in SQL operator within the
where clause here. So it's selecting all
of the related objects that are in a set
of related values. So that's select and
load. So this is a vital loading
strategy with SQL Alchemy and it can
greatly improve performance in your
applications and it prevents that n plus
one problem. Now I mentioned it earlier
on that we can actually define this
strategy on the relationship itself. So
let's see how to do that just now on the
reviews property on this movie model. So
when we define the relationship, I'm
going to split this into multiple lines,
one for each parameter. And if we want
to define a default strategy, we can use
the lazy keyword argument and you can
see the default value here is select.
But what we can use, and by the way we
can see all the possible values using
this, and we'll look at a couple of
these in later videos. The one we are
going to use is select in and that's
going to then use that select and load
strategy by default. So let's save
models.py and we can now go back to the
notebook. And what I 'm going to do is
remove the where clause. So we don't
need that anymore. But this options call
that we're doing here and passing in the
strategy of select and load for
movie.reviews. We actually don't need
this anymore either. So we can remove
this because we've now added it to the
model relationship. So it's now declared
as the default loading strategy when we
access reviews. So if we now go back to
the notebook, what we can do is execute
this selection and we're going to see if
we go below here that we are no longer
getting a huge number of SQL queries
being executed. Instead, we only have
that simple select in operation that we
saw before and that is now occurring by
default when we get the movies out of
the database. Now, we should caveat this
with the fact that you might not always
want to get the related objects in a
subsequent query. There might be a lot
of times where you just want to access a
particular model and you don't want to
preload all of the related objects for a
particular field. So, it's not always
the case that you want to use the select
in strategy, but it is one of the most
common and it is the one that you're
going to find yourself using the most to
prevent that n + 1 problem. And we can
either define that strategy directly on
the relationship field or as we saw
before, we can use the dot options
method on a selection to specify what
the selection or rather what the loading
strategy should be for a particular
related field. Now, we're going to look
at another loading strategy in the next
video and that is the joined load
strategy.
